<section class="page-hero"><h1>Rice University, Houston, Texas</h1><p class="lead">Guest teaching stay · Department of Transnational Asian Studies</p></section>
<main class="content"><div class="content-inner fieldwork-story rice-story">
<figure class="fieldwork-hero"><img src="data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAIAAAAAAAP///ywAAAAAAQABAAACAUwAOw==" data-rice-img="01" alt="Rice University campus in Houston" loading="eager"><figcaption>Rice University in Houston: a campus whose brick-and-stone architecture frames an institution deeply connected to the intellectual history of the city.</figcaption></figure>
<p class="lead">My stay at Rice University in Houston was one of the highlights of my time in the United States. Invited by Professors <a href="https://profiles.rice.edu/faculty/shih-shan-susan-huang" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Shih-shan Susan Huang</a> and <a href="https://profiles.rice.edu/faculty/eric-huntington" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Eric Huntington</a>, I had the opportunity to teach, exchange ideas with students, and present my research in an environment where art history, Buddhist studies, and transnational approaches to Asia are constantly in conversation. By the end of the stay, I already felt that I was leaving too soon two mentors and interlocutors whose generosity had made the experience possible.</p>
<h2>Rice, Houston, and Asian studies</h2>
<p>Chartered in 1891 as the William M. Rice Institute and opened to students in 1912, the institution became Rice University in 1960. Today this private research university holds a prominent place in American higher education; Rice's institutional overview notes that it is consistently ranked among the top twenty universities in the United States by <em>U.S. News</em>. Its campus, residential college system, and proximity to the Texas Medical Center give it a distinctive identity within an exceptionally international metropolis.</p>
<div class="rice-pair"><figure><img src="data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAIAAAAAAAP///ywAAAAAAQABAAACAUwAOw==" data-rice-img="08" alt="Arcades on the Rice University campus" loading="lazy"><figcaption>The campus arcades, one of Rice's immediately recognizable architectural settings.</figcaption></figure><figure><img src="data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAIAAAAAAAP///ywAAAAAAQABAAACAUwAOw==" data-rice-img="02" alt="Group photograph with colleagues at Rice University" loading="lazy"><figcaption>With colleagues and members of the Rice community: many of the most valuable conversations continued well beyond the classroom.</figcaption></figure></div>
<p>Houston gives this teaching a particular resonance. Rice's Kinder Institute estimates that in 2023 more than 655,000 Asian residents lived across the four principal counties of the metropolitan region, representing 9.9 percent of the population, compared with 1.8 percent in 1980. The Vietnamese community is particularly significant. Teaching Vietnamese art history in Houston therefore did not mean speaking about a remote and abstract place: histories of migration, religious heritage, and cultural circulation discussed in class are also part of the social fabric of the city.</p>
<h2>Teaching Korean and Vietnamese art history</h2>
<p>In Susan Huang's seminar <em>Art and Heritage of East Asia</em>, my sessions focused on the art history of Korea and Vietnam. My aim was to place these traditions within an East Asian history that is not organized only from China or Japan: following transfers, local appropriations, Buddhist networks, court cultures, and forms of heritage allows Korea and Vietnam to emerge as active agents in the production and circulation of images.</p>
<div class="rice-pair rice-lecture-pair"><figure><img src="data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAIAAAAAAAP///ywAAAAAAQABAAACAUwAOw==" data-rice-img="03" alt="Lecture on a Guan Yu sanctuary in Saigon" loading="lazy"><figcaption>A session on Vietnam, here discussing a Guan Yu sanctuary in Saigon and the religious and visual circulations that crossed East Asia.</figcaption></figure><figure><img src="data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAIAAAAAAAP///ywAAAAAAQABAAACAUwAOw==" data-rice-img="04" alt="Lecture on Độc Lôi Sơn temple in Nghệ An" loading="lazy"><figcaption>Presenting Vietnamese material around the đền Độc Lôi Sơn in Nghệ An.</figcaption></figure></div>
<p>These sessions were also an opportunity to think about how to teach objects that national categories explain only imperfectly. A temple, painting, statue, or ritual practice may be deeply embedded in a local history while carrying models, texts, and iconographies that travelled over very long distances. This tension between rootedness and circulation is precisely what makes the art history of East Asia so productive.</p>
<div class="rice-pair rice-classroom-pair"><figure><img src="data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAIAAAAAAAP///ywAAAAAAQABAAACAUwAOw==" data-rice-img="05" alt="Rice University seminar seen from the back of the classroom" loading="lazy"><figcaption>In seminar at Rice: discussion with students was an essential part of the stay.</figcaption></figure><figure><img src="data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAIAAAAAAAP///ywAAAAAAQABAAACAUwAOw==" data-rice-img="09" alt="Presenting in a seminar at Rice University" loading="lazy"><figcaption>Working through visual case studies made it possible to move constantly between formal analysis and religious, social, and political contexts.</figcaption></figure></div>
<h2>Buddhism, gender, and artistic patronage</h2>
<p>At Eric Huntington's invitation, I also contributed to his seminar <em>Buddhism and Gender</em>. I presented the role of women in commissioning Buddhist artworks in Korea, not as a peripheral topic but as a question that requires us to reconsider how histories of artistic production are written. Inscriptions, votive texts, and court contexts allow us to recover female patrons and to trace the familial, religious, and political networks through which images were financed, offered, consecrated, and transmitted.</p>
<p>This approach connects directly with my research on Korean court Buddhist art. Looking at works through their patrons prevents us from reducing them to a succession of styles or schools: they become material traces of devotional strategies, social relationships, family memories, and positions within the court. Discussing these questions in a seminar devoted to gender opened particularly stimulating comparisons with other Buddhist traditions.</p>
<h2>An experience that was human as much as academic</h2>
<div class="rice-pair"><figure><img src="data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAIAAAAAAAP///ywAAAAAAQABAAACAUwAOw==" data-rice-img="06" alt="Informal moment with colleagues at Rice University" loading="lazy"><figcaption>The conversations naturally continued outside the classroom.</figcaption></figure><figure><img src="data:image/gif;base64,R0lGODlhAQABAIAAAAAAAP///ywAAAAAAQABAAACAUwAOw==" data-rice-img="07" alt="Memory of the stay outside a seminar room at Rice University" loading="lazy"><figcaption>A memory from the stay outside the seminar room, after several days of teaching and discussion.</figcaption></figure></div>
<p>What I remember most from Rice is the quality of the welcome and the conversations. None of this stay would have had the same meaning without Susan Huang and Eric Huntington, whom I warmly thank for their invitation, trust, and generosity with their time. I also thank the entire teaching staff and the whole Department of Transnational Asian Studies team for such a warm welcome. The stay reminded me that an academic invitation can become much more than a sequence of classes: it can become a space of dialogue, comparison, and intellectual friendship that continues to nourish research long after returning home.</p>
